title: As his own soul (1 Samuel 18:1–4)
hook: Jonathan loves David as his own soul and gives him his robe

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shepherd with a sling and no armor walked out to meet a giant. Your line was one was enough. What big thing did you face with small tools? Today, someone standing near the king was watching him. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

The fight is over. David stands in front of King Saul, and Saul asks him a plain question: whose son are you? David answers, the son of your servant Jesse, from Bethlehem. That's all he says, as far as the text tells us. But someone else is in the room. Jonathan, the king's son. A fighter himself, the one who once climbed a rocky pass with only his armor-bearer beside him to face a Philistine camp. Later in the book, Saul will tell him outright that as long as David lives, Jonathan's own kingdom won't be secure. Jonathan has every reason to see this shepherd as a rival. And when David has finished speaking, the text turns away from the king and looks at his son.
screen: `WHOSE SON ARE YOU?` → `JONATHAN IS LISTENING.` → `THE KING'S SON, AND A RIVAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening of chapter eighteen. The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, "and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." The Hebrew word under soul is nefesh, and it's wider than the English. It can mean life, breath, the self that's alive in you. So Jonathan loves David the way a person holds on to their own life. And the phrase doesn't come once. Two verses later, Jonathan makes a covenant with David, a binding promise, and the reason given is the same: because he loved him as his own soul. Then he does something with his hands. He strips off the robe he's wearing and gives it to David. Then his garments. Then his sword, his bow, his belt. Everything a prince and a soldier would wear into a room, he hands to a shepherd. The text doesn't explain the gesture. Some readers hear the heir to the throne quietly handing over what marks him as heir. Others hear something simpler: a friend dressing his friend in the best he has. Either way, nothing comes back the other direction. David gives nothing in these verses. The rabbis noticed this friendship. In Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, there's a teaching about love. Love that depends on some thing ends when the thing is gone. Love that doesn't depend on anything never ends. And the example they give of the second kind is the love of David and Jonathan: a friendship that isn't about what the other person can do for you.
screen: `KNIT, SOUL TO SOUL.` · `NEFESH: LIFE, BREATH, SELF.` · `THE ROBE, THE SWORD, THE BOW.` · then, large: `AS HIS OWN SOUL.` · then: `LOVE THAT DEPENDS ON NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a friend something of yours. Settle, and breathe. Let one friend come to mind, someone whose life you'd hold close. Then look around your own life for something to hand them. Not something you were throwing out. A book you love. A jacket. An hour. A thing you made. A skill you could teach. Choose one, and picture putting it in their hands. Notice whether part of you wants to hold it back, and let that be there too. If you pray, you can hold the verse: he loved him as his own soul. The bell holds the time.
nefesh. The Hebrew word for soul or self, wide enough to hold how Jonathan loved David, giving him his robe and his sword. Today's word.
Your line: love that doesn't end. Today, give that one thing away, and don't ask for anything back. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Jews read the friendship of David and Jonathan in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and the teaching in Pirkei Avot about love that depends on nothing is studied with it.

fork.setup: you're Jonathan, the king's son. a shepherd has just become the hero of the army. what do you do?
options: keep your distance: he's a rival.
give him your robe, your sword and your bow.
ask your father to send him home.
fork.reveal: Jonathan strips off his robe and hands it over, with his garments, sword, bow and belt, and makes a covenant with David.

original.note: Hebrew: as his soul, from nefesh, life or self, in 1 Samuel 18:1 and 18:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: two young men become good friends.
what it means: the king's son loves a possible rival as his own life, binds himself to him, and gives him his robe and weapons.
what a scholar hears: Pirkei Avot holds up David and Jonathan as its example of love that depends on nothing, and so never ends.
recall: the glory is departed from Israel
